sentences.text: Where was he coming from?
New York.
This meeting is being recorded.
Okay.
Just letting all the AIs in.
Great.
Yeah, thank you for picking up the couple of emails that we've sent you and be happy to talk you through what it is that we do.
And our client, and they're the job for us really is just to kind of get to know you a little bit better and see if there's a fit and if you're in a position really to talk about being acquired.
My client is obviously keen to make a number of acquisitions again this year.
We made two of them last year and they've got about three in the pipeline at the moment, so very acquisitive.
So I'll just tell you a little bit about us.
We're capital A, we're an M and A advisory and we work both on the buy and the sell side with marketing services, services companies.
So all of our clients are either agencies themselves or they're investors or private equity firms that are acquiring these types of companies.
So in this instance, these guys are actually private investors but have made a number of investments now.
So they are looking to build on the agencies that they've acquired.
They're a company called Skyview Innovations and they acquired a company called Hovercraft Studio and another one called Irma.
But Hovercraft are quite well known, particularly in the immersive space.
So I don't know if you've come across them before, but quite a few people that we speak to have.
But I see you, you work mostly in sort of the luxury sector.
So they were really right across lots of different brands, but they do quite a bit of sport and you know, some mid level brands as well.
So yeah, really the nature of these calls, just to find out a little bit about where you are at at the moment and what your interest level is of being part of a larger company.
And yeah, my main goal really is to get you on a call with our client and see if there's chemistry.
Yeah, it's very compelling.
So, you know, we're a fairly young agency.
We're about three and a half essentially.
I.
My career has been in experiential, primarily for fashion, beauty and luxury.
So I worked in agency for six years.
I was.
Well, more like 10 years between several different agencies.

And then I went in house at Tom Ford Beauty for four years and then out of that I launched this agency and we've been doing very well, particularly with the Estee Lauder companies, you know, because I worked internally there.
We started working with Essentially all of their brands and they've been our bread and butter for the past few years.
They are having a substantial financial slowdown.
So we have been diversifying and bringing in more mass brands like Chobani.
But you know, for a lot of reasons this year isn't the large year that last year was.
Essentially we went from like 1.3 million to 5 million to 8 million last year.
And so this year it doesn't look like we'll hit 8 million, but I think that's a lot because our bread and butter client is not spending the way they were.
And also there's some economic factors.
So as I mentioned, we're taking the time to diversify.
We are really interested in a few things from a consumer facing perspective.
We obviously work in the beauty space already, fashion space adjacent.
We're trying to bring in more mass brands.
We're working with Chobani, we want to bring it.
We're trying to work with the Rockettes and you know, we'd like to bring in even larger mass brands.
And then on the B2B side we want to target tech, finance and pharmaceutical for some of their internal conferences because those are quite robust budgets.
Yeah, that's interesting.
Yeah, because hovercraft, they work with Nike for instance, but they also with Coinbase as well, so.
Oh, nice.
Yeah, kind of already doing that, that sort of thing.
Not really working with the luxury brands, but certainly those mass brands and the, the financial one.
So what is the type of work that you kind of specialize in?
I can see you're doing very sort of high end experiential stuff.

Yeah, so a lot of our work has been around product launches and influencer destination events where you know, you bring a group of influencers to some interesting location that connects with the storytelling of the product and give them like a two to four day experience around that.
Know that's what we did for La Mer in San Diego, that's what we did for Estee Lauder in Costa Rica and in Palo Alto at Stanford.
So that's one of the things we do well.
We also, you know, in our portfolio and certainly in my body of work is this, those larger immersive builds.
I did a lot of that work with Tom Ford.
We continue to do some of that work.
And so we're actually actively seeking out clients that are more build focused.
You know, we think we've got this like high touch, influencer, experiential down.
And so we want to add to that with more like large immersive builds.
Right.
And what's the sort of strategy around that?
Is that just because there's more budget there or is it because you guys sort of specialize it in some of the tech or, or you can just see better margins?
I mean, what is it that you're looking for there?
Yep.
So it's, it's, there's definitely more budgets when it comes to building out a space.
And as a creative agency, it allows us to flex our muscles better and I think then have better.
It's not like portfolio work but like outward facing credentials to that end.
One of the points of difference we had have is that we, we have an elevated, we have a very elevated esthetic that also can marry well to the brands.
We work to integrate technology into all of those builds either through digital, mobile or AR or AI.
And then we also are, we also deal in adaptation as it pertains to different markets.
Right.
And you've, you seem to have grown quite quickly in three and a half years.
Yes.
Is that just down to your, your great network?
I mean you guys are obviously extremely experienced in the brands space that you're in.

Yeah, it's primarily because of the network, the, the existing network that I had within the Estee Lauder companies and other fashion and beauty houses, which is why now that luxury is, you know, not pushing as hard as it is.
We're trying to diversify into things that will keep us budgetarily solid and allow us to do some of that, you know, really press worthy work that doesn't, that maybe the margins aren't as high on.
Right.
But so far we've had pretty good margins.
We end up about 20%.
We've actually increased our agency fee to 25% so we can really hit that between 20 and 22% by the time the project's over.
And was there a lot of exposure to just Estee Lauder and their brands then?
Was there some client concentration around them?
Yeah, there was a considerable amount.
We were basically running to keep up with them for the past three years.
We also did work with Chanel for the past three years on some of their smaller events.
You know, the, a friend, a friendly agency that we know does all of their big events.

So we're obviously not like going for that business, but we were doing some of their smaller beauty suites for their consumer events and some of their artistic endeavors like talkbacks, their film talkbacks and literary conversations.
Yeah, but we, but essentially to be totally transparent, we've been running to keep up with Lauder for the past three years.
Right.
Well, what Just a sort of rough estimate.
What do you think they are in terms of like percentage of your revenue?
They were like 70% of our revenue.
Wow.
Well, it's a lot of SD money.
It was hence the need to actively diversify.
Right.
Okay, cool.
All right, look, there is a, there's a real risk around that with a buyer.

And so I just want to be really transparent that although I know possibly what's happened is you've kind of divided and conquered within them as you've gone, you've probably taken on more and more brands.
So in reality it probably isn't a huge risk.
But what it does sometimes do is reduce the value of an agency because it just becomes a big risk.

If for some reason, like for instance, there was this thing with Fox before they were acquired by Disney, there was a lot of companies that were exposed the same way and then when Disney acquired them, they just shut Fox's relationships down, all of those agencies.
And so it was a risk.
There was actually one, that one that came true.
But quite often those companies can go for years and years with having like 100 different, you know, smaller brands and not really exposing that agency to a huge amount of risk.
But I'm just being transparent that it might be, might be an issue later when it, when it comes to valuation.
And then like.
So your strategy around events, because I can see that you actually do immersive strategy or experiential strategy as well.
Yes.
Yeah.
What are you looking to do there?

So I should imagine the beauty stuff and I'm just being a little bit naive, but I imagine the beauty stuff just needs to look beautiful and it's probably just really high end locations and things like that.
But is there anything else that you have to definitely get there in terms of the tech and the mobile and the AR stuff, fun stuff that you're including on purpose.
Yeah, the strategy itself is more of like a larger global strategy for a calendar year.
So for example, a brand comes to us, they're like, we want to start doing events.
We don't exactly know what to do.
Can you give us some options?
And, and what we tend to do is craft the event strategy or the strategy for one particular launch.
But it in a 360 way, how it links to social media, how it links to out of home, how it links to like CRM.
So that's really as far as strategy is concerned.
That's where our strengths lie.
Not only in telling people like, oh, you should have you thought of this format or this format?
And so are you Connecting it to the other touch points within your organization.
You know what, what is your social.
Is your social team capturing content around this?
Like how are they putting paid marketing behind it?
So that's really what the strategy piece is.
And then our next pillar obviously is creative direction and design, which we are happy to do with execution or without execution.
You know, we're first and foremost a creative agency.
So you know, the creative is part of the currency.
And then of course we've got full service production and project management and execution.
So those are really like the three pillars.
You can have all of them.
You can have one of them, you.
Know, would you say makes up the sort of the strategy piece and the piece where you're just doing creative and you don't do any of the execution?
It's small, it's smaller than I'd like.
I would be like to do much more strategy and creative concepting around that strategy.
Of course we always want to execute it.
But, but you know, those projects are incredibly high margins because there's almost no expenses as it pertains to like putting together decks or proof of concept things.
Yeah.
So you know, I would like to be doing a lot more of that work.
Yeah, the strategy is the good stuff.
Yep.
Yeah.
As you grow, you still, you, you end up going back to, to, to get the delivery done as well and pick up as as much of the budget as possible.
So.
Yeah.
Okay, brilliant.
And then just on your, your profit margin.
So I know you said you bounced up a couple of times and then back down, but what's your margins like?
Good.
Profitable.
You in debt?
Anything else like that?
No, we're, we currently, right now we're, we have extended our credit more than we're comfortable with.
But typically we operate always profitably.
We've never lost money and our margins end up being somewhere between like 18 and 22% at the end of the day.
Right.
That's before operating expenses of course.
Right.
So that's gross profit you mean?
Okay.
And so, so net profit, do you have an idea where that is in terms of percentage?
Yeah, net profit falls to probably like 11 and that's primarily due to like tax optimization.
Okay.
Yeah.
And there's, there's a lot of, you know, when you're delivering large events for, for big brands, there's a lot of expense, isn't there, at the top end?
So.
So yeah, all good.
Yeah, we tend to put all of the, as much of the project expense onto the project budget.
So you know, we're running like 18 to 22 sometimes 25% for the project and then our operating budget is completely separate from that.
Like the only things really are like insurance and legal that could be deemed as a project expense.
But literally everything else, staffing, sometimes even internal staffing, all of that goes onto the project budgets.
All of our taxis, any kind of meals, it's all on the project budget.
Right.
Okay, brilliant.
And then in terms of yourself, what is your current ambition?
Is it just you that's the owner of the business or are there other shareholders?
I'm the exclusive owner.
What's your current aspirations for the business?
What are you looking to do?
Frankly, I want to continue to grow and diversify the experiential side of things.

Bringing in clients that really bolster the bottom line regardless of, regardless of like notoriety so that we can take on some of those more public facing projects and not have to worry about the bottom line as much.
And at the same time we're making like, we're adding on to it entertainment services.
So we've all like most of our team has an entertainment background.
So the goal in you know, seven to 10 years is that we're acquiring intellectual property, developing new works for television, film and theater and working with group of artists.
Like a group of talent.
Rather not artists, but like talent to develop their careers as well.
So it's really like going into a multi, multi avenue kind of entertainment company with experiential at one as one arm.
Yeah, yeah, I call that 360 degrees.
So you kind of own your own audience as well as being able to deliver the services and, and everything else.
So you got the content as well in the ip?
Exactly.
Okay, so I guess you've got quite a long term vision if you're thinking about that already.
If you were to, to be made an offer, I mean do you, do you think about exiting or selling the business or being part of a, a larger business at all?
I would, I would be very interested to know what the arrangement would be, what the agreement would be as far as like how this company transitions into a larger company.
If they're looking to retain leadership or if they're just looking for the owner to exit.
From my perspective I could stay and guide or I could take the payout and leverage that into a completely new endeavor.
It does not matter to me, you know.
So just to give you a bit of general background.
So very, very generally, most acquisitions are made with the intent to keep the founder in for as long as possible really.
But in practice it's usually a three year earn out can sometimes Be as long as a five year earn out.
With these guys in particular, they're looking to acquire talent like yourself.
You know, they want really super creative leadership.
And particularly because hovercraft is growing so quick, they have so much work, they're doing 5 million plus EBITDA and they're growing exponentially and they've got a ton of work coming.
They need more delivery capacity as well.
So they're looking for people like yourself that can be able to take that off their hands and lead and deliver projects as well.
So certainly they wouldn't be looking for something like yourself to exit.
No, that's good.
I would prefer, I would prefer to stay.
You know, as you mentioned, I have a long term vision.
So whether or not that happens within or without, like I still do want to guide the ship that I created.
And that could be something that sort of works well after you've kind of got through the journey with this.
Because what they're looking to do is build a business that's worth hundreds of millions and exit out within the next three or four years.
And yeah, it's generational wealth what they're trying to create.
And I say trying, but these are very experienced guys that have done it multiple times before.
So they've done it in the cloud computing space and they can see a trend that's moving in the immersive space.
That's very similar technology as well.
You've probably spotted it yourself.
So that's what they're trying to build around and they're bringing that huge wealth of experience with them to have one last go at it before they retire permanently to the golf course.
Really?
I guess.
Amazing.
Yeah.
My goal really is just to get those kind of details from you and see whether you would feel comfortable getting on a call with them.
So, yeah, we'll report back to them on.
My next meeting is due Wednesday next week, but I'm updating them daily.
So are you going to be around over the next sort of.
Yes, we have a, we have a project in Oregon next week.
So basically there, the 10th is not a good day.
But outside of that it's possible.
But you know, frankly until the 11th, I'm kind of in production.
Okay.

All right, well I'll take that information as well and let's see what we can, we can get set up to have that initial call and then both sides get to see if there's chemistry and if it's something you want to be part of, then we can continue.
Thank you.
Pleasure meeting you, Joseph.
Sounds really what a great business.
Thank you.
Thanks for giving us a call.
Yeah, no worries.
So.

summary.overview: The Initial Exploratory Acquisition Discussion meeting between Joseph Lucius and Andy Day focused on an potential acquisition of Joseph's experiential marketing agency by Skyview Innovations. Andy introduced his firm, Capital A, which specializes in M&A advisory for marketing services and highlighted Skyview's intention to expand its portfolio after previous acquisitions. Joseph detailed his agency's growth from $1.3 million to $8 million in revenue over three years, though he noted a recent decline due to challenges with Estee Lauder Companies, from which they derive 70% of their revenue. The agency specializes in high-end experiential events and aims to diversify its client base, with a strategic focus on expanding service offerings that yield higher margins. Joseph expressed openness to acquisition provided that leadership retention is possible, while Andy outlined typical earn-out terms and the overarching goal of Skyview to build a multi-million-dollar business for a future exit. Next steps include reporting the conversation to Skyview and arranging a follow-up meeting while accommodating Joseph's availability post-10th.
summary.short_summary: Joseph Lucius and Andy Day held a discussion regarding the potential acquisition of Joseph's experiential marketing agency by Skyview Innovations. Andy, representing Capital A, emphasized Skyview's strategy to expand its portfolio after previous acquisitions, while Joseph detailed his agency's impressive growth from $1.3 million to $8 million in revenue over three years, despite a recent decline attributed to challenges with Estee Lauder Companies, which accounts for 70% of their revenue. The agency specializes in high-end experiential events and is seeking to diversify its client base and enhance service offerings for higher margins. Joseph expressed a willingness to entertain the acquisition, contingent on retaining leadership, while Andy outlined typical earn-out terms and Skyview's goal of building a multi-million-dollar business for a future exit. They agreed to report back to Skyview and arrange a follow-up meeting, considering Joseph's availability post-10th.
